strengths: The paper identifies a real gap in RVOS: many referring expressions are relational and require distinguishing actor and target roles, while most existing RVOS datasets and models treat the referent as an isolated object. The proposed InterRVOS formulation is useful and well motivated.

InterRVOS-8K is potentially valuable in scale and coverage: 8,738 videos, 35,247 objects, 127,314 expressions, and 17,682 actor-target interaction samples, with single-object, multi-object, motion-only, and interaction-aware expressions.
The annotation pipeline is described in reasonable detail, including the four stages and the prompts used for GPT-4o/LLaMA generation in the appendix, which helps transparency.
The baseline ReVIOSa is simple and task-aligned: adding role-specific [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens to an MLLM+SAM2 segmentation framework is a natural design for actor-target segmentation.

The experiments support that the dataset and model are useful: InterRVOS-trained models improve zero-shot MeViS performance over Ref-SAV in Table 3, ReVIOSa improves over Sa2VA on InterRVOS-8K in Table 5, and the joint actor-target ablation improves J&F from 53.8 to 59.7 in Table 6.
weaknesses: The largest concern is annotation validity. The dataset is fully automatic, but the paper does not report a human audit, error rate, inter-annotator check, or validation of interaction labels, actor/target roles, generated expressions, or masks. Since the dataset is the main contribution, this missing evidence materially weakens the claims.

The manuscript does not clearly explain how ground-truth segmentation masks are obtained from the VidOR source data. It repeatedly claims corresponding masks and mask tracks, but the construction section focuses on captions/interactions and gives no adequate mask-generation or mask-quality protocol.

Several shown dataset examples raise quality concerns, e.g. awkward or semantically questionable expressions such as “Person holding for black and brown dog,” “person handing to person,” and “Person explaining to person and car.” These are not just presentation issues because they suggest noisy supervision and possibly ambiguous actor-target labels.

The evaluation is partly circular: the InterRVOS test set, expression categories, and actor-target labels are produced by the same automatic pipeline family used to create the training data. Without a human-labeled interaction benchmark or manual test subset, it is hard to know whether gains reflect genuine interaction understanding rather than matching annotation style.

Baselines may not be fully comparable in the actor-target setting. Existing RVOS methods are designed for a single referred mask, while ReVIOSa is explicitly trained to emit two role masks. The paper needs a clearer protocol for adapting baselines and ensuring the comparison is fair.

The architecture contribution is incremental. ReVIOSa mainly adds two special segmentation tokens and joint supervision on top of existing MLLM/SAM2-style systems; the novelty lies more in the task/dataset than in the modeling.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The pipeline relies on proprietary GPT-4o, a quantized LLaMA model, filtering heuristics, and unspecified details such as learning rate, optimizer, frame sampling, exact train/validation split construction, and data release status. The abstract also leaves the project page blank.

The writing and framing contain inconsistencies: the task is described as requiring paired expressions, but the model is said to segment actor and target from a single expression; VidOR is incorrectly associated with the YFCC100M citation in one place; and there are frequent grammatical issues. These do not invalidate the work, but they obscure important technical details.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful gap in RVOS: many real video queries are relational and require distinguishing actor and target roles rather than segmenting a single isolated object. The task formulation and actor-target evaluation protocol are potentially useful for future work.

The proposed InterRVOS-8K dataset is large in terms of videos, objects, expressions, and reported interaction expressions, and the paper provides a reasonably transparent multi-stage prompting pipeline with prompts in the appendix.

The empirical results suggest that interaction-centric data can improve transfer to MeViS and other RVOS benchmarks, including zero-shot settings. The reported gains over Ref-SAV and Sa2VA are nontrivial in several tables.

The baseline model is simple and practical: adding actor/target segmentation tokens to an MLLM plus SAM2-style segmentation stack is a natural extension, and the ablation indicates that joint actor-target supervision helps more than using independent tokens.
weaknesses: The central dataset contribution is insufficiently validated. InterRVOS-8K is automatically generated by GPT-4o/LLaMA, but the paper provides no human audit of caption correctness, interaction-role correctness, actor-target assignment accuracy, or mask quality. Since the benchmark itself is generated by the same pipeline, reported performance may reflect learning annotation artifacts rather than genuine interaction understanding.

The source and construction of segmentation masks are unclear. The paper says the dataset is built from VidOR and provides mask tracks, but it does not explain how pixel-level masks are obtained from VidOR-style annotations, how mask errors are filtered, or how temporal mask consistency is ensured. This is a serious reproducibility and technical-validity gap for a segmentation benchmark.

The evaluation has a circularity concern: the proposed model is trained and evaluated on automatically generated interaction expressions and role labels from the proposed pipeline. Without a manually verified test set or external interaction-aware benchmark, the claims about actor-target understanding are not strongly supported.

The novelty of the model is limited. ReVIOSa mainly adds [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens to an existing MLLM/SAM2 framework, while relying on strong pretrained components. The paper does not isolate whether gains come from the architecture, the data distribution, the base model choice, or prompt/token formatting.

Comparisons are not fully convincing. Some baselines are trained on different data sources and scales, and the paper does not clearly establish matched training budgets, identical backbones, or equivalent access to the proposed training data for all competitors. The 4B ReVIOSa also barely improves over the 1B version, which raises questions about robustness of the claimed architecture benefit.

Several dataset examples expose quality problems in the generated language and roles, e.g., awkward or semantically odd expressions such as “Person holding for black and brown dog,” “person handing to person,” and “Person explaining to person and car.” These examples weaken confidence in the annotation pipeline, especially without quantitative quality control.

The task definition is somewhat inconsistent: the paper alternates between paired expressions, single interaction expressions, actor-only/bidirectional cases, and joint actor-target output from one prompt. It is not always clear exactly what input/output contract is being evaluated in each setting.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as exact split construction, filtering criteria, prompt sampling, decoding settings, mask generation, model hyperparameters beyond batch/epochs, and code/data availability are either missing or only lightly described. The project page placeholder also appears blank in the extracted manuscript.

The writing and presentation contain many grammatical errors, citation inconsistencies, and imprecise claims. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they make already subtle dataset and evaluation details harder to verify.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful gap in RVOS: many referring expressions are relational, yet existing datasets and protocols mostly evaluate isolated actor-only segmentation. The proposed InterRVOS task, with actor-target expressions and role-specific masks, is a natural and useful extension for video understanding.

InterRVOS-8K appears valuable in scale and scope: 8,738 videos, 35,247 objects, 127,314 expressions, and 17,682 actor-target interactions. The dataset includes single-object, multi-object, motion-only, and interaction-aware expressions, which should be useful beyond the proposed baseline.

The annotation pipeline is described in reasonable detail and the appendix includes prompts, model choices, clip extraction, dataset statistics, and qualitative examples. This helps make the automatic construction process more transparent than many LLM-annotated dataset papers.

The empirical evidence supports the central claim that interaction-centric data is useful. Training Sa2VA on InterRVOS-2K/5K improves zero-shot MeViS performance over Ref-SAV despite fewer videos, and InterRVOS-5K improves results across multiple caption types on the proposed evaluation set.

The proposed ReVIOSa baseline is simple but well matched to the task. The actor/target token design has a clear ablation: joint [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] modeling improves overall J&F from 53.8 to 59.7 on InterRVOS-8K, and ReVIOSa outperforms Sa2VA baselines on the new actor-target evaluation.
weaknesses: The largest concern is annotation reliability. The dataset is automatically generated using GPT-4o and LLaMA, but the paper does not report human verification, inter-annotator agreement, precision/recall of detected interactions, or an error taxonomy. Since the main contribution is a dataset, evidence that actor-target roles and generated expressions are correct is essential.

The evaluation set is also automatically constructed from the same source and pipeline, which raises a risk of measuring compatibility with the annotation procedure rather than robust interaction understanding. A human-curated validation subset or evaluation on an independent interaction-oriented benchmark would strengthen the claims.

The model contribution is comparatively incremental: ReVIOSa mainly adapts an existing MLLM/SAM2 segmentation framework with two special tokens. This is sensible and effective, but the architectural novelty is modest relative to the dataset contribution.

Some reported gains are moderate or mixed. ReVIOSa-4B only slightly improves over ReVIOSa-1B overall on InterRVOS-8K, and in zero-shot standard benchmarks the InterRVOS-trained Sa2VA sometimes outperforms ReVIOSa. This does not undermine acceptance, but it tempers claims that the architecture broadly improves video understanding.

Reproducibility is not fully established. The abstract says a project page is available, but the URL appears blank in the manuscript. The pipeline also depends on proprietary GPT-4o annotations, and more precise release details for data, masks, generated captions, splits, and training code are needed.

The manuscript has presentation issues, including grammatical errors and awkward phrasing, and some generated expression examples are ungrammatical. These are mostly fixable, but they also hint at possible dataset language-quality issues that should be quantified.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of standard RVOS: interaction expressions often imply asymmetric actor and target roles, but existing formulations typically segment only a single referred actor or object set. The InterRVOS task definition and actor/target evaluation protocol are well motivated and potentially useful for video-language grounding and interaction understanding.

InterRVOS-127K is a substantial dataset contribution, with 127K expressions, separate actor-target annotations for 17.6K interaction expressions, and a human-refined evaluation set. The staged annotation pipeline is described in unusual detail, including prompts, source data, clip extraction, and dataset statistics, which improves reproducibility relative to many dataset papers.

The proposed ReVIOSa design is simple but appropriate for the task: separate [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens naturally match the role-specific output structure, and the attention mask loss is supported by ablations showing gains from both components. On InterRVOS-127K, ReVIOSa-4B improves actor J&F over the strongest reported baseline from 71.3 to 74.5 and provides target segmentation with 68.3 J&F.

The work also checks compatibility with standard RVOS benchmarks. ReVIOSa remains competitive or strong on MeViS, Ref-Youtube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS, and the dataset transfer experiments suggest the interaction-centric data may improve general video-language grounding rather than only overfitting the new benchmark.

The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful figures, qualitative examples, and extensive appendix material documenting the annotation process, AML head/layer selection, and additional evaluations.
weaknesses: The central dataset is automatically annotated using SAM2, GPT-4o, and LLaMA, but the paper provides limited quantitative validation of annotation quality. The evaluation set is said to be human-refined, yet there is no reported correction rate, inter-annotator agreement, role-label accuracy, mask quality audit, or breakdown of common failure modes. Since the main benchmark and training data are both produced by this pipeline, label reliability is a material concern.

The target-segmentation evaluation lacks meaningful external baselines. Existing RVOS methods are marked inapplicable for InterRVOS-Target, but the paper does not compare against reasonable adaptations such as running a strong RVOS model separately on actor/target noun phrases, prompting an MLLM-based model to output two masks, using grounded conversation/phrase grounding baselines, or training Sa2VA-like architectures with two segmentation tokens. This makes it hard to isolate the benefit of ReVIOSa from task-specific supervision and output formatting.

The method contribution is relatively incremental beyond the new task/data: adding two special tokens and supervising selected attention heads is sensible, but not deeply novel. AML head/layer selection also appears empirically tuned on the same setting, and the paper does not fully address whether the selected attention supervision generalizes across architectures, datasets, or prompts.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. For example, improved actor segmentation is interpreted as evidence of better interaction dynamics, but the experiments do not directly test interaction reasoning, role reversal robustness, causal role understanding, or cases where actor and target have similar appearance. The qualitative examples are useful but do not substitute for targeted stress tests.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the detailed prompts. Important training details such as learning rates, optimizer settings, frame sampling, loss weights, thresholding/post-processing, and exact baseline fine-tuning protocols are either missing or not easy to locate. The abstract mentions a project page but no usable URL is visible in the manuscript text.

The dataset is derived from VidOR and interaction statistics show only 17.6K actor-target expressions out of 127K total expressions. The paper would be stronger with more analysis of interaction categories, long-tail coverage, multi-object interaction handling, and whether performance varies by interaction type, object count, directionality, or active/passive expression form.

strengths: The paper identifies a reasonable limitation of standard RVOS: many referring expressions involve asymmetric interactions, and segmenting only the actor can ignore semantically important target objects. The actor/target formulation is potentially useful for more relational video-language understanding.

The proposed InterRVOS-127K dataset is large in scale, with 127K expressions, 35K objects, and 17.6K actor-target interaction annotations. The paper also includes a clear high-level annotation pipeline and human refinement of the evaluation split.

The model design is simple and aligned with the task: separate [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens are a natural extension of MLLM-based RVOS models, and the attention mask loss is supported by ablations showing gains over the baseline configuration.
The paper reports several useful secondary evaluations, including standard RVOS benchmarks and zero-shot comparisons, which partially address whether the dataset/model help beyond the new benchmark.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too self-contained. The main claim of interaction-aware segmentation is validated primarily on the authors' own automatically generated dataset, with no independent interaction-centric benchmark or manually annotated external test set. Strong performance on InterRVOS-127K may reflect alignment with the authors' annotation pipeline rather than genuine interaction understanding.

The baseline comparison for the new task is weak. Existing RVOS methods are marked as not applicable for InterRVOS-Target, but the paper does not evaluate straightforward adaptations such as prompting the target noun phrase, running a single-[SEG] model separately for actor and target, using passive/active paraphrases, or training comparable baselines on the same actor-target annotations. This makes it difficult to attribute gains to the proposed architecture rather than to task-specific output formatting.

Dataset quality is insufficiently characterized. The training set is automatically annotated using GPT-4o/LLaMA and SAM2 tracks, but the paper provides no quantitative audit of annotation correctness, role-direction correctness, mask quality, failure modes, or inter-annotator agreement for the human-refined evaluation split. Since the dataset is the central contribution, this is a material weakness.

There is a risk of linguistic shortcut learning. The pipeline generates paired active/passive expressions and assigns actor/target roles from structured captions; examples such as 'person handing to person' and 'car being worked on by person' may allow models to infer roles from generated language templates rather than from video interaction dynamics. The paper does not test robustness to paraphrases, role swaps, ambiguous expressions, or expressions where visual evidence is required to determine the direction of interaction.

The proposed model contribution is fairly incremental. Separate segmentation tokens and a BCE supervision loss on selected attention heads are plausible but not especially novel, and the selection of top attention heads appears empirically tuned on the same setting. The reported ablation supports utility, but not a deeper technical advance.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. Important settings such as learning rates, optimizer, frame sampling, SAM2 variant, LoRA rank, loss weights, prompt format, exact train/validation construction, human refinement protocol, and annotation filtering criteria are missing or under-specified. The dependence on closed GPT-4o annotations also makes exact dataset regeneration difficult.

Claims of state-of-the-art performance should be tempered. On standard RVOS benchmarks the method is competitive but mixed, e.g. it improves MeViS over Sa2VA but is lower on Ref-DAVIS, and the main SOTA claim is on the newly introduced dataset where competing methods are not fully adapted to the task.

The writing is understandable but contains many grammatical issues, repeated claims, and some unclear table descriptions. More importantly, some explanations are vague, such as how the model decides at inference whether an expression is interaction-based and how target masks are evaluated for multi-target interactions.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful gap in RVOS: many referring expressions describe asymmetric interactions, but standard RVOS evaluates only the referred actor and ignores target objects. The InterRVOS task and actor/target evaluation protocol are well motivated and could be useful for fine-grained video-language understanding.

InterRVOS-127K is a substantial contribution: 127K expressions over 8,738 videos, with 17,604 actor-target interaction expressions and separate actor/target masks. The appendix provides useful annotation-pipeline details, prompts, examples, and dataset statistics.

The proposed ReVIOSa design is simple and well aligned with the task: separate [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens map naturally to role-specific segmentation, and attention mask loss is a plausible auxiliary grounding signal.

Empirical evidence is generally positive. ReVIOSa-4B achieves the best reported performance on the new benchmark for actor segmentation and provides target segmentation results where prior RVOS methods are not directly applicable. The paper also shows competitive transfer to standard RVOS benchmarks, including MeViS and Ref-Youtube-VOS.

The ablations support the main architectural choices: interaction-aware tokens and AML each improve over the baseline, and their combination gives the largest gain. The attention analyses provide a reasonable mechanistic motivation for AML.
weaknesses: The dataset is heavily automatically generated using SAM2, GPT-4o, and LLaMA, but the paper gives limited quantitative validation of annotation quality. The evaluation set is said to be human refined, yet there are no reported error rates, inter-annotator agreement, or statistics separating expression errors from mask errors.

The strongest novelty is the task/dataset rather than the model. ReVIOSa is largely an adaptation of an MLLM plus SAM2 segmentation pipeline with two role-specific tokens and an auxiliary attention loss; this is sensible but not deeply novel architecturally.

The evaluation against prior methods is somewhat incomplete for the new target-segmentation setting. Existing baselines are marked inapplicable for target masks, but the paper does not include strong adapted baselines, such as decomposing interaction expressions into actor/target prompts, adding two segmentation tokens to a baseline, or using noun-phrase grounding models to segment both entities.

Some claims about interaction understanding are stronger than the evidence. Improved actor J&F may reflect additional supervision or better training data rather than genuine modeling of inter-object dynamics; the paper provides limited diagnostic tests for role reversal, ambiguous interactions, multi-object target assignment, or directionality errors.

Ablation reporting is narrower than desirable. The main ablation table appears to report a single RVOS-style score rather than separate actor and target performance, making it hard to judge how much each component improves the specifically interaction-aware capability.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The appendix includes prompts and high-level training details, but key implementation details such as complete hyperparameters, loss weights, sampling strategy, exact baseline training protocol, and release status are not sufficiently explicit. The abstract also references a project page but does not provide a usable URL in the manuscript text shown.

Presentation has several grammatical issues and some ambiguous terminology, especially around actor-only RVOS versus interaction-aware evaluation. These do not undermine the main contribution but do reduce clarity.
